questions.q: Aldehydes are more reactive than ketones towards nucleophilic addition because:
questions.solution:
Two effects work the same way. A ketone has **two** alkyl groups releasing electrons to the carbonyl carbon, reducing its positive character; and those two groups **crowd** the approaching nucleophile.

An aldehyde has one alkyl group and one hydrogen, so it is both more electrophilic and more accessible.
options: of less steric hindrance and less electron release to the carbonyl carbon

questions.q: Tollens' reagent distinguishes aldehydes from ketones by forming:
questions.solution:
An aldehyde reduces ammoniacal silver nitrate to metallic silver, which deposits as a **silver mirror** on the tube wall.

Ketones do not react, because oxidising them would mean breaking a carbon–carbon bond.

Fehling's solution is the other classic test, giving a red-brown $\text{Cu}_{2}\text{O}$ precipitate — but aromatic aldehydes do not respond to it.

questions.q: The iodoform test is given by:
questions.solution:
A yellow precipitate of $\text{CHI}_{3}$ forms with $\text{I}_{2}$/NaOH from a **methyl ketone** or a methyl carbinol (which is oxidised to one in the conditions).

So ethanal and acetone give it, but propanal and propanone's higher homologues do not. Ethanol gives it; methanol does not.

It is a test for a particular *fragment*, not a functional group — which is why it is so useful in structure determination.
options: compounds containing the $	ext{CH}_{3}	ext{CO}-$ group or $	ext{CH}_{3}	ext{CH(OH)}-$ group

questions.q: Which of these is the strongest acid?
questions.solution:
Each chlorine withdraws electrons inductively, spreading the carboxylate's negative charge and stabilising it.

Three chlorines do this three times over, so **trichloroacetic acid** is the strongest ($\text{p}K_{a}$ $0.7$, against acetic acid's $4.76$ — nearly ten thousand times stronger).

The effect falls off sharply with distance: a chlorine three carbons away barely matters.

questions.q: The Cannizzaro reaction is given by aldehydes that:
questions.solution:
An aldehyde **without an $\alpha$-hydrogen** cannot undergo aldol condensation, so with concentrated alkali it **disproportionates** instead — one molecule is oxidised to the acid, another reduced to the alcohol.

$2\text{HCHO} + \text{NaOH} \to \text{CH}_{3}\text{OH} + \text{HCOONa}$

Benzaldehyde and formaldehyde are the standard examples.

questions.q: Find the molar mass of acetic acid, $\text{CH}_{3}\text{COOH}$, in g/mol. (C $= 12$, H $= 1$, O $= 16$.)
How many aldehyde and ketone isomers together are possible for $\text{C}_{4}\text{H}_{8}\text{O}$ (open chain, carbonyl compounds only)?
questions.solution:
Butanal, 2-methylpropanal and butanone — $\mathbf{3}$.

Two aldehydes and one ketone. Aldehydes and ketones of the same formula are **functional isomers**.

questions.q: Find the degree of unsaturation for benzoic acid, $\text{C}_{7}\text{H}_{6}\text{O}_{2}$.
questions.solution:
$\dfrac{2(7) + 2 - 6}{2} = \dfrac{10}{2} = \mathbf{5}$.

Four from the benzene ring and one from the $\text{C}{=}\text{O}$ of the acid group.

questions.q: How many moles of NaOH are needed to neutralise one mole of oxalic acid, $\text{HOOC–COOH}$?
questions.solution:
Oxalic acid is **dibasic** — two $-\text{COOH}$ groups, so $\mathbf{2}$ moles of NaOH.

Counting the acidic hydrogens rather than the total is the point of the question.

questions.q: How many of these give a positive Tollens test: ethanal, propanone, benzaldehyde, methanoic acid?
questions.solution:
**Ethanal** ✓ (an aldehyde), **benzaldehyde** ✓ (an aldehyde), **methanoic acid** ✓ (it contains a $-\text{CHO}$ group and is the one carboxylic acid that reduces Tollens').

**Propanone** ✗ — a ketone.

So $\mathbf{3}$. Formic acid's dual character catches most students out.

questions.q: Explain the aldol condensation with a mechanism, and state which compounds can undergo it.
questions.solution:
**Which compounds.** Any aldehyde or ketone with at least one **$\alpha$-hydrogen**.

**Reaction.** With dilute alkali, two molecules of ethanal give a $\beta$-hydroxy aldehyde (an 'aldol'), which loses water on warming:

$2\text{CH}_{3}\text{CHO} \xrightarrow{\text{dil. NaOH}} \text{CH}_{3}\text{CH(OH)CH}_{2}\text{CHO} \xrightarrow{\Delta} \text{CH}_{3}\text{CH}{=}\text{CHCHO} + \text{H}_{2}\text{O}$

**Mechanism.**

**Step 1.** The hydroxide removes an $\alpha$-hydrogen, giving a **carbanion** stabilised by resonance with the carbonyl (an enolate). This is why the $\alpha$-hydrogen is essential — and why it is acidic at all.

**Step 2.** The carbanion attacks the carbonyl carbon of a second molecule.

**Step 3.** Protonation gives the aldol.

**Step 4.** On heating, dehydration gives a conjugated $\alpha,\beta$-unsaturated carbonyl compound — the extra stability of the conjugation is the driving force.

**Cross aldol** between two different carbonyl compounds gives four products and is only useful when one partner has no $\alpha$-hydrogen.

questions.q: How would you distinguish between: (a) an aldehyde and a ketone, (b) acetaldehyde and acetone, (c) a carboxylic acid and a phenol?
questions.solution:
**(a) Aldehyde from ketone.**

**Tollens' reagent:** the aldehyde gives a silver mirror; the ketone does not.

**Fehling's solution:** the aliphatic aldehyde gives a red-brown precipitate of $\text{Cu}_{2}\text{O}$; the ketone gives nothing. (Aromatic aldehydes do not respond.)

**(b) Acetaldehyde from acetone.** Both are methyl compounds, so both give iodoform — that test will not separate them.

Use **Tollens' or Fehling's**: acetaldehyde reacts, acetone does not.

**(c) Carboxylic acid from phenol.**

**Sodium bicarbonate:** the acid gives brisk **effervescence** of $\text{CO}_{2}$; phenol does not, being too weak an acid to displace carbonic acid.

**Neutral $\text{FeCl}_{3}$:** phenol gives a violet colour; most carboxylic acids give a buff precipitate.

The bicarbonate test is the cleanest single distinction in organic chemistry: it separates acids stronger than carbonic acid from everything weaker.

questions.q: Describe three methods of preparing carboxylic acids, and three of their important reactions.
questions.solution:
**Preparation.**

1. **Oxidation of primary alcohols or aldehydes** with acidified $\text{KMnO}_{4}$ or $\text{K}_{2}\text{Cr}_{2}\text{O}_{7}$:

$\text{RCH}_{2}\text{OH} \to \text{RCHO} \to \text{RCOOH}$

2. **Hydrolysis of nitriles:**

$\text{RCN} + 2\text{H}_{2}\text{O} \xrightarrow{\text{H}^{+}} \text{RCOOH} + \text{NH}_{3}$

Useful because it **adds a carbon atom** to the chain.

3. **From Grignard reagents:**

$\text{RMgX} + \text{CO}_{2} \to \text{RCOOMgX} \xrightarrow{\text{H}^{+}} \text{RCOOH}$

Also chain-lengthening, and it works where nitrile hydrolysis will not (tertiary and aryl acids).

4. **Oxidation of an alkyl benzene** side chain: toluene gives benzoic acid, whatever the chain length.

**Reactions.**

1. **With bicarbonate** — $\text{CO}_{2}$ evolved (the identifying test).

2. **Esterification** with an alcohol and a trace of acid — a reversible reaction driven by removing water.

3. **Reduction** with $\text{LiAlH}_{4}$ to the primary alcohol. $\text{NaBH}_{4}$ is not strong enough.

4. **Hell–Volhard–Zelinsky reaction** — $\text{Cl}_{2}/\text{red P}$ substitutes at the $\alpha$-carbon, giving $\alpha$-halo acids, the gateway to $\alpha$-amino acids.

5. **Decarboxylation** — the sodium salt heated with soda lime loses $\text{CO}_{2}$ to give an alkane one carbon shorter.

questions.q: Write the mechanism of the addition of HCN to a carbonyl compound, and explain the role of the base.
questions.solution:
**Step 1 — generating the nucleophile.** A trace of base converts HCN into the cyanide ion, which is a far better nucleophile:

$\text{HCN} + \text{OH}^{-} \rightleftharpoons \text{CN}^{-} + \text{H}_{2}\text{O}$

**Step 2 — attack.** $\text{CN}^{-}$ attacks the electrophilic carbonyl carbon. The carbon changes from $sp^{2}$ to $sp^{3}$ and the $\pi$ electrons move onto the oxygen, giving an alkoxide.

**Step 3 — protonation.** The alkoxide takes a proton from HCN, giving the cyanohydrin and regenerating $\text{CN}^{-}$.

$\text{R}_{2}\text{C}{=}\text{O} + \text{HCN} \to \text{R}_{2}\text{C}(\text{OH})\text{CN}$

**The base's role.** Pure HCN reacts extremely slowly; adding base speeds it up enormously, because the reaction depends on $[\text{CN}^{-}]$, not on $[\text{HCN}]$.

That kinetic observation is the evidence for the mechanism — the nucleophile is the ion, not the molecule.

**Why cyanohydrins matter:** the nitrile can be hydrolysed to an $\alpha$-hydroxy acid or reduced to an amine, so this one step lengthens the carbon chain and installs a new functional group.

questions.q: Explain why carboxylic acids are more acidic than phenols and alcohols.
questions.solution:
**The comparison.** $\text{p}K_{a}$: acetic acid $4.76$, phenol $10$, ethanol $16$.

**Carboxylate resonance.** On losing a proton, the carboxylate's charge is shared between **two equivalent oxygen atoms**. The two resonance structures are identical, which gives the maximum possible stabilisation, and both C–O bonds become the same length — confirmed by X-ray measurements.

**Phenoxide** delocalises its charge too, but onto **carbon** atoms of the ring, which hold a negative charge far less willingly, and those structures disrupt the aromatic sextet. The stabilisation is real but much weaker.

**Alkoxide** has no delocalisation at all, and the alkyl group actually pushes electrons towards the already-negative oxygen, making things worse.

**The principle.** The more the conjugate base is stabilised, the more readily the acid gives up its proton. Acidity is decided by what is left behind, not by the O–H bond itself.
